title: Project-Based Learning

pts: A project runs across multiple lessons toward a substantial outcome, with learners exercising real choice and ownership.
This scales Unit 11's unit-sequencing principles specifically toward project-based, rather than lesson-based, structure.
The outcome should resemble something learners might genuinely produce outside the classroom.

v: Descriptions of six classroom activities on cards

items: Give pairs of teachers six cards, each describing a classroom activity (see model language).
Sort them into three groups: single task, unit of work, project.
For each ‘project’, check it against four questions: Does it run across several lessons? Do learners make real choices? Is there a substantial outcome? Would the outcome exist outside school?
Improve one weak ‘project’ so that it passes all four questions.
Share improved versions.
Teachers bring a project they have set in the past and test it against the four questions.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A. Learners write a letter to a pen friend in one lesson.
B. Learners copy pictures of national symbols onto a chart at home.
C. Over four weeks, groups survey their street about water use and present a leaflet to the panchayat.
D. Over five lessons, learners read a story, study the past tense and write an ending.
E. Groups choose a local craft, interview a craftsperson and make a short guidebook for visitors.
F. Learners give a two-minute talk about their favourite food.

blocks.x: C and E are projects. B is a common ‘project’ in name only: no choice, no inquiry, no English, and often done by an adult. Improved version of B: groups choose one symbol, find out one surprising fact from two sources, and present it on a class ‘Did you know?’ wall, with a spoken explanation.

body: Figure 36.1 One task, one unit, one project

Purpose: to show the difference in scale. Content: three horizontal bars on a timeline of weeks. The first is a single short block labelled ‘task’; the second, a row of five blocks joined by arrows labelled ‘unit’; the third, a long arc across several weeks with small flags for stages, ending in a star labelled ‘real outcome’. Style: clean, diagrammatic. Board version: three lines of increasing length.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared list of past projects and improvements.

blocks.x: Activity cards and chart paper in a staff meeting.

pts: Planning, research and data collection, analysis and production, and presentation form the typical project arc.
Each stage draws on different skills, naturally integrating them across the project's full length.
This mirrors Unit 11's cumulative-task principle, expanded across several weeks rather than one unit.

items: Introduce the project goal and final outcome (for example, a school newsletter).
Show a map of four stages: planning, research, production, presentation.
With the class, list what each stage will involve and which skills it will use.
Agree dates for each stage and mark them on the map.
Display the map and tick off stages as the project moves on.
For a shorter project, combine research and production into one stage.
Support: provide a partly completed map with the stages already filled in.
Challenge: groups plan their own sub-deadlines within each stage.

blocks.x: A project map for ‘Our School Newsletter’ (Class 8, five weeks):

lines: Week 1, Planning: choose sections, assign roles (reading, speaking, writing).
Weeks 2–3, Research: interview teachers and staff, take notes, collect facts (listening, speaking, note-making).
Week 4, Production: draft, peer-edit and finalize articles (reading, writing).
Week 5, Presentation: read extracts at assembly; distribute copies (speaking).

blocks.x: Each stage uses a different combination of skills, so integration happens naturally across the project, as the cumulative task in Unit 11 did within one unit.

body: Purpose: to show the typical project arc. Content: a road with four milestones labelled ‘Plan’, ‘Research’, ‘Produce’, ‘Present’; small icons at each (a list, a magnifying glass, a pencil, a microphone), and skill labels under each milestone. Style: bright, map-like. Board version: four boxes joined by arrows.

items: Trello (free plan) or Google Sheets (free) for a digital stage tracker.

blocks.x: The project map on chart paper, displayed on the wall.

pts: Genuine choice over topic or approach within the project raises motivation more than any imposed topic reliably can.
This connects directly to Unit 22's self-efficacy and motivation research.
Structure choice within clear boundaries — open but not unbounded — to keep the project feasible.

items: Set a fixed frame: the theme, the time, the final form and the language focus.
Inside the frame, offer genuine choices: topic, sources, roles and form of presentation.
Groups discuss options, using their home languages if they wish, and write a short proposal in English.
Approve each proposal, or ask for one change to make it feasible.
Groups sign their proposal; it becomes their contract.
Groups propose a completely new topic, if they can justify it within the theme.
Support: a proposal template with sentence starters.
Challenge: proposals must include a research question and two sources.

blocks.x: A choice board, theme ‘Water in our community’:

lines: Topic: rainwater harvesting / a local lake / water at home / water and farming.
Source: interview / survey / newspaper / observation.
Outcome: leaflet / poster exhibition / short radio programme / guided walk.

Our group will find out how families in our street save water. We will survey ten families and interview one farmer. We will make a leaflet with five tips. Roles: Meena, questions; Arif, notes; Kavya, design; Sunil, presenter.

blocks.x: Choice raises motivation because it supports learners’ sense of autonomy (Ryan and Deci 2000); the frame keeps the project achievable.

body: Purpose: to show bounded choice. Content: a picture frame labelled ‘Theme, time, outcome’, containing four open windows, each showing a different group working on a different topic. Style: warm, colourful. Board version: a rectangle divided into four windows.

items: Google Forms (free) for groups to submit proposals.

blocks.x: A choice board on the blackboard and a paper proposal form.

body: Stoller (1997) described a ten-step sequence for project work in which the teacher and learners agree on a theme, determine the final outcome and structure the project before gathering, compiling and presenting information. Several of the steps are explicit language-preparation steps, placed just before learners need that language.

pts: Build in interim checkpoints across the project's length, similar to Unit 11's mid-unit formative check.
Without checkpoints, weaker time-management skills can derail an otherwise strong project by the final stage.
Checkpoints should assess progress and process, not just anticipate the final product.

v: A checkpoint card for each group

items: Set checkpoints at the end of each stage (roughly weekly).
At each checkpoint, meet each group for five minutes while others continue working.
Ask about progress (what is done?) and process (how did you work? what problems arose?).
Record agreed next steps on the group’s checkpoint card.
Follow up at the next checkpoint.
In a class of 50, meet group leaders only, who report back to their groups.
Support: more frequent, shorter checkpoints for groups that struggle with planning.
Challenge: groups run their own checkpoint review and submit the card.

lines: What have you finished since last week?
What is left to do, and who is doing it?
What problem did you meet? How did you solve it?
What English do you need for the next stage?
Week 2. Done: 8 of 10 surveys. Problem: two families not at home. Next: Arif asks the teacher next door. Language needed: reporting numbers (‘Six out of ten families…’).

body: Purpose: to show checkpoints. Content: a long path with flags at regular points; at each flag, a teacher sits briefly with a small group, and a card shows ‘done’, ‘next’, ‘problem’. Style: friendly, practical. Board version: a line with four flags.

items: Google Classroom (free) for groups to post checkpoint updates.

blocks.x: A checkpoint card clipped to each group’s folder.

body: Hold checkpoints while the rest of the class is working on a clear, independent stage of the project. Five minutes with each of eight groups fills most of a lesson, so plan checkpoints on days when groups have enough to do.

pts: Plan explicit language-focus sessions tied to what the project stage currently demands, not a fixed pre-set syllabus.
This connects to Unit 28's language-focus stage, scaled to recur across a project rather than a single task.
Anticipate common language needs (reporting findings, describing a process) and prepare support proactively.

items: Before the project, list the language each stage will demand.
Plan short language-focus sessions just before the stage that needs them.
Teach from examples: a model interview, a model report, a model leaflet.
Learners practise briefly, then use the language in their project work.
Notice new gaps during the project and add sessions as needed.
Groups identify their own language needs at each checkpoint and request a mini-lesson.
Support: phrase banks on cards for each stage.
Challenge: learners compare two models and draw out the features themselves.

lines: Planning: suggesting and agreeing (Why don’t we…? That’s a good idea, but…).
Research: asking questions politely (Could you tell me…? How often do you…?).
Analysis: reporting findings (Most families… Only two out of ten… The survey shows that…).
Production: describing a process (First, collect the water. Then…).
Presentation: signposting (We will talk about three things. Finally…).

blocks.x: The language-focus stage of the task cycle (Unit 28) recurs here, several times, each time tied to a real need.

body: Figure 36.5 The right language at the right time

Purpose: to show language support tied to stages. Content: the project road from Figure 36.2, with a small toolbox appearing just before each milestone, each labelled with a language function. Style: clear, consistent with Figure 36.2. Board version: stages with a phrase written under each.

items: Padlet (free plan) for a shared phrase bank that grows during the project.

blocks.x: A phrase chart on the wall, added to at each stage.

pts: Assess the final product, the working process across the project, and the presentation of results as distinct components.
This distributes assessment weight beyond only the polished final output, which favours only certain learner strengths.
This previews Unit 42's portfolio and Unit 43's collaborative-assessment work, both compatible with project assessment.

items: Share a rubric with three parts at the start: product, process and presentation.
Assess process at each checkpoint, using the checkpoint cards.
Assess the product when it is submitted.
Assess the presentation on the day.
Give each learner a short feedback note naming one strength and one next step in each part.
Learners self-assess against the rubric before the teacher does.
Support: fewer, simpler criteria.
Challenge: learners help to write one criterion in each part.

blocks.x: A simple rubric (written for this book):

lines: Product: content is accurate; the purpose is clear; language suits the reader.
Process: meets deadlines; shares work; solves problems; uses feedback.
Presentation: clear structure; audible; answers questions.

blocks.x: Assessing the three parts separately rewards learners whose strengths lie in organization or collaboration, not only those who write polished English. Unit 42 (portfolios) and Unit 43 (collaborative assessment) develop these ideas further.

body: Purpose: to show distributed assessment. Content: a roof labelled ‘Project grade’ resting on three pillars labelled ‘Product’, ‘Process’ and ‘Presentation’, each with three small criteria written on it. Style: architectural, simple. Board version: three columns under a triangle.

items: Google Sheets (free) for recording scores across checkpoints.

blocks.x: A printed rubric in each group folder.

pts: Unit 34's cooperative-learning principles matter even more over a multi-week project, where group tension has more time to develop.
Build in periodic group processing checkpoints specifically for interpersonal dynamics, not just task progress.
Have a clear, fair process for addressing unequal contribution before it damages the group's outcome.

items: Once a week, give each group a card with four questions about how they are working together.
Each member answers individually (a tick, a cross or a question mark).
The group discusses the answers and agrees one improvement.
Collect cards and notice any group with repeated problems.
If one member is contributing much less, meet the group, hear each member, and agree a fair plan.
Use a ‘contribution log’ in which each member records what they did each week.
Support: questions in the home language alongside English.
Challenge: groups write their own group agreement at the start.

lines: Did everyone have a job this week?
Did everyone speak in our meetings?
Did we listen to each other’s ideas?
Is anyone doing too much or too little?

blocks.x: A fair process for unequal contribution:

lines: 1. Listen to the group and to the individual separately. 2. Look for the reason (absence, a difficult role, conflict). 3. Agree a specific task and deadline. 4. Check at the next checkpoint.

blocks.x: Over several weeks, small tensions have time to grow. The cooperative-learning principle of group processing (Unit 34; Johnson, Johnson and Holubec 1994) matters even more here.

body: Purpose: to show group processing. Content: four learners sitting around a card with four questions and smiley, straight and puzzled faces beside each. A small arrow points to ‘One thing to improve’. Style: gentle, supportive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) for an individual, private contribution check.

blocks.x: Group health cards in the group folder.

points.h: When a Project Goes Off Track
pts: Projects run longer than lessons and are more vulnerable to derailing — build contingency time into the schedule from the start.
A mid-project checkpoint that reveals a group is behind should trigger a scoped-down outcome, not abandonment.
This connects to Unit 9's timing-and-contingency principle, scaled to the length of a full project.

items: Build one spare lesson into the project map from the start.
At the mid-point checkpoint, identify groups that are behind.
For each, agree a smaller outcome that keeps the project’s core purpose.
Record the change and adjust assessment fairly.
After the project, note what caused delays and plan for them next time.
Keep a bank of ‘scoped-down’ outcomes ready for common problems.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Planned: a 12-page newsletter. Behind: only four articles drafted. Scoped-down: a 4-page newsletter with a front page, two articles and a puzzle.
Planned: a video tour. Problem: no phone available. Scoped-down: a spoken tour, performed live, with a hand-drawn map.

blocks.x: Unit 9 argued that a lesson plan needs contingency time. A project needs it more. Exams, holidays and power cuts are predictable interruptions; plan for them.

body: Figure 36.8 A shorter route to the same place

Purpose: to show scoping down. Content: a map with a long road to a mountain-top flag labelled ‘Planned outcome’, and a shorter path branching off to a lower hill with a flag labelled ‘Scoped-down outcome’. A group of learners takes the shorter path, still smiling. Style: hopeful. Board version: two routes to two flags.

items: Google Calendar (free) for key dates and a spare lesson.

blocks.x: The project map, with a spare lesson marked in a different colour.

body: Run a short two-week ‘mini-project’ before attempting a full one. Choose a simple outcome, such as a class survey reported on one poster. Note where the time went and which stage needed most support. Use what you learn to plan a longer project next term.

dek: Unit 36 of 100: scaling task-based principles across weeks instead of one lesson, toward a substantial, learner-driven outcome with real-world resemblance.

aims.x: This unit stretches the task cycle of Unit 28 across several weeks. A project is a sequence of linked tasks that leads to a substantial outcome which learners have chosen, shaped and own. The unit shows how to plan the arc of a project, support language along the way, keep groups working well, and assess fairly, all within the realities of large classes and a crowded syllabus.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what distinguishes a project from a single task or a unit of work;
plan a project through its typical stages, from proposal to presentation;
offer learners genuine choice within clear, feasible boundaries;
build checkpoints that monitor process as well as progress;
plan language-focus sessions that respond to what each stage demands;
assess product, process and presentation as separate components;
manage group dynamics and unequal contribution over several weeks;
rescue a project that has gone off track by scoping it down.

why: Why this matters. A single task proves integration works in one lesson. A project proves it can sustain motivation and skill development across a much longer arc.

background.x: Project work has a long history in education, reaching back to Kilpatrick’s ‘project method’ in the early twentieth century and the experiential philosophy of John Dewey. In language teaching it became prominent in the 1980s and 1990s, when teachers looked for ways to give communicative activity a larger purpose than the single lesson. Diana Fried-Booth’s Project Work (2002, first published 1986) and Tom Hutchinson’s Introduction to Project Work (1991) offered practical models in which learners plan, gather information, produce something and present it. Legutke and Thomas (1991) placed projects within a wider view of the classroom as a place of shared experience and learner responsibility.

Fredricka Stoller (1997) identified features that make projects valuable for language learners: a focus on content rather than on isolated language points; learner-centredness, with the teacher as guide; cooperation alongside individual effort; the integration of skills; and an end product that is shared with others. Reviews of project-based learning in general education (Thomas 2000) and in second language education (Beckett and Miller 2006) report gains in motivation, autonomy and language use, while also noting that projects demand careful structure. Without it, the language learning can be thin, and a few learners may do most of the work. Motivation research gives a reason why ownership matters: self-determination theory holds that autonomy, competence and relatedness support intrinsic motivation (Ryan and Deci 2000), and Unit 22 showed how success builds self-efficacy.

The Indian policy context is supportive. The National Education Policy 2020 calls for experiential and inquiry-based learning, and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023 treats projects as a normal part of learning across the stages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Many schools already set projects, but often as homework that parents complete or as copied charts. An English project done in class, with stages, checkpoints and language support, is different. Learners can also use their home languages to plan, interview and research, then produce in English: a survey of grandparents’ childhood games might be conducted in Kannada or Urdu and reported in English. Home languages then become a resource for real inquiry rather than something to hide.

A project does not replace the coursebook. It can run alongside it for one or two lessons a week, or take the place of a coursebook unit whose theme it shares. This unit builds on Unit 11, which showed how lessons build towards a unit outcome, and on Unit 34, which set out the principles of cooperative learning.

items: Checkpoint record. Review checkpoint cards for evidence of process: meeting deadlines, solving problems, using feedback.
Product rubric. Assess the outcome against criteria shared at the start.
Presentation. Assess structure, clarity and response to questions, separately from the written product.
Individual reflection. Each learner writes a short note: what I did, what I learned, what I would change.
Which ‘projects’ in your school are really homework charts? How could one be turned into a real project?
How much genuine choice do your learners have in their English lessons?
How would you know if one learner were doing most of a group’s work?
Which language needs could you predict for your next project?
What interruptions should you plan for in your school calendar?
How could learners’ home languages support their research?

terms.def: Giving learners real choices, such as the topic of a project, within limits set by the teacher, such as a theme, time and required outcome.
A planned review point during a project at which the teacher and group check progress and process, give feedback and adjust plans before continuing.
A record in which each member of a group notes what they did each week on a project, supporting fair individual assessment and accountability.
In cooperative learning, time for groups to reflect on how well they worked together and what to improve, for example at the end of a task.
Learners’ sense that a task or project genuinely belongs to them, fostered by giving real choices over topic, roles or outcome within agreed limits; ownership tends to increase effort and commitment.
Assessment of how learners work over the course of a project, such as planning, collaboration and problem-solving, rather than only the final product.
Assessment of the final outcome of a project or task, such as a poster, report or presentation, against clear criteria.
The final product of a project, such as a poster, video, report or presentation, which gives the work purpose and an audience.
An approach in which learners work over an extended period on a project that produces a real outcome, integrating language skills with research and collaboration.

Reducing the planned outcome of a project to something achievable when time or resources run short, rather than abandoning it. A class planning a full magazine might produce a single-page newsletter instead.
